name: Expo
summary: A React Native application platform that supplies native modules, generates and configures native projects, and distributes JavaScript and asset updates within a compatible native binary boundary.

features.name: Cross-platform native module API
features.description: The Expo Modules API lets applications and libraries define native capabilities and views in Swift and Kotlin behind a JavaScript-facing module surface. Expo documents comparable behavior across Android and iOS and integration with React Native's modern architecture.
benefits: Reduces boilerplate for exposing platform capabilities to JavaScript
Provides a consistent module and view lifecycle across mobile platforms
Allows reusable native functionality to be packaged independently of an app
costs: Native platform behavior and permissions remain part of module design
The abstraction adds a dependency on Expo's module runtime and conventions
Lower-level C++ integrations may still require a different React Native boundary

features.name: Config-plugin native project generation
features.description: Expo config plugins transform app configuration and apply platform-specific mods during prebuild. In continuous native generation projects, this makes native project changes reproducible from configuration instead of requiring direct edits to generated iOS and Android files.
benefits: Reapplies native configuration during regeneration and CI builds
Keeps library-specific native setup close to the library configuration contract
Separates app intent from platform file-editing details
costs: Plugin ordering and platform-specific mods can affect generated output
Unsupported native customizations may require manual projects or custom plugins
Generated files are an output and should not be treated as the sole source of intent

features.name: Binary-compatible over-the-air updates
features.description: EAS Update serves JavaScript, styling, and image changes through expo-updates to an installed app. The documented boundary excludes native code, native dependencies, permissions, and SDK changes, which require a new app binary.
benefits: Delivers compatible JavaScript and asset fixes between store submissions
Allows channels, rollouts, and republishing of a known update
Makes the native binary a stable execution boundary for supported updates
costs: Updates must remain compatible with the installed native binary
Native changes still require build, signing, and store distribution workflows
Update selection, rollback, and adoption add release-state operational concerns

mathematical_views.question: How do app configuration, plugin functions, platform mods, and generated native projects compose into a build input?
assumptions: App configuration is the source node and generated native files are derived nodes
Plugin and mod edges are ordered transformations with platform-specific effects
The view abstracts Xcode, Gradle, and compiler behavior after generation

mathematical_views.question: Which application changes can transition through an OTA update, and which require a new native binary?
assumptions: A binary declares the native capabilities and runtime compatibility available to an update
JavaScript and asset changes are modeled as update payloads
Native code, permissions, and SDK changes transition to a new-build path rather than being proven safe by the model

benefits: Reusable native capabilities with a consistent JavaScript-facing contract
costs: Platform permissions, lifecycle details, and runtime dependency remain visible

benefits: Repeatable native setup from declarative app and library configuration
costs: Plugin composition and generated-output debugging add build-system complexity

benefits: Fast delivery of compatible JavaScript and asset changes
costs: Compatibility limits prevent OTA delivery of native capability changes
